sections.heading: ### Hear the Guard First
sections.why: After your exchange (the question, what the part might say, your reply, and which voice to use), each paragraph is one thing the guard might do, or, the first, how you earn its trust, so a reader can go straight to theirs.
old: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?"

It might say this will just be one more performance, and you'll fool yourself again. That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo! If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.
A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that's been in your way. I'd still keep the Nurturer voice. If that voice isn't there in you yet, borrow it from someone who's been safe for you.

A new roommate doesn't win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector earns that guard's trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.

That part doesn't have to move out. It's been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one. I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there's a grown-up here now who could call it all off if things got to be too much. It doesn't have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I'd listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.

If it's been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn't want to get mine up either. I'd tell it something like, "You don't have to hope yet, I'll keep coming back even when I mess up." Sometimes it doesn't say anything back for a while.

Blaming yourself can be doing a protective job, too. "It's all my fault" might be your parent's line, word for word. Then again, if it's your fault, maybe you can fix it before they leave. I'd stop the cruelty either way. And I'd get curious about what makes it so hard to give up.

sections.heading: ## Start With Whatever Showed Up
sections.why: After the path (what showed up, what to ask it, your line to say, and waiting), each paragraph is one of the things that can happen next. Your answer paragraph held two of them, a feeling to be present for and an instruction to be careful with, so it splits, and "How you picture all that is up to you" moves up three sentences to sit right after the forms an answer can take, which it is about. What to make of a fear or a stray thought gets its own paragraph.
old: You might go looking for your little one and get mad instead, or realize you've been staring at the rug. I count that as pl/ork too, even if it feels like it's in the way. Before you decide where it's coming from, ask it what it's trying to stop, or what it wants. Maybe it just has something to say. It could be your little one, mad that you took so long to come back, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. Maybe it's that parent you inherited, or something from earlier today, or a bit of each.
You can tell that part something like, "I see you. I'm not going to force my way past you. What's going on?" Or however you'd actually say that. Then wait and listen patiently.

If nothing comes, that's fine for now. No need to answer for that part just because you'd set this up as a healing session. Even without the answer, you can notice what sets the reaction off, and you can understand what the reaction is propelling you toward, and away from.

Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It's often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that's what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what you actually know.

How you picture all that is up to you, as long as it helps, and the simpler the better. I think a fear that keeps turning up to tell you something is worth talking to as a part of you. If it sounds like your little one, though, hear it out the first time it shows up. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you're in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it's your little one asking.

I wouldn't spend long deciding what to call each part, though. Every part of you learns from how the others treat it, your little one included. A part of you that's trying to protect you might warn you about something, and when you hear it out, it doesn't have to get any louder.

Anxiety is often a part of you that's trying to protect you, making a guess about what's coming, like that people will laugh at you. It can be right! It's probably been wrong before too, and you know some of those times. Unless it might be real danger, or something a doctor should look at, I'd go see.
If a part hesitates about being touched or about sex, or says no to going deeper in this work or to an altered state, I'd stop there and not test it, even when it sounds like a prediction.

sections.heading: ### When to Change the Strategy
sections.why: Your first paragraph is the general case, nothing much changing; each one after it is a different reason to change course, and your last paragraph holds two of them.
old: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I’d want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never have to find out what's underneath this. Before going with either of those paths, look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes the strategy was not actually implemented, just read about or played around with lightly. Or there wasn't the right environment to really practice it, like no alone time. Or perhaps you did sit down with your little one, but it felt scary or like some part of you was trying to protect you from going deeper. Whatever it turns out to be, it makes sense to work on that blocker instead of giving up on everything.

Maybe the words are all there, but the loving grown-up behind them isn’t, not yet. Some people at that point might try saying sweeter and sweeter things, and then upon that not working, perhaps just “throw the baby out with the bathwater,” and decide reparenting is a scam. I’d borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.

Let's say an exercise leaves you feeling lighter for a few hours, but then the old feeling comes back later on. Some relief is nice, but we still want to know if we are fixing the problem at a deeper level and integrating the benefits into regular life (like texting a friend that you're having a rough day rather than saying you're fine). Jot down what changed and how long it lasted. Although if that feeds into your OCD patterns, drop it.

How many tries would I give it? It's not like we can just put a number on it. Some things shift in a day. Others take about as long as learning guitar. But do notice if progress is stagnating. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts).

Not wanting to do it anymore might be reason enough, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first to get a better understanding. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it!

sections.heading: ## When Escape Leaves Reality Behind
sections.why: After your opening on doses and protocols, each paragraph is its own warning, so a reader can find theirs: a trip that went badly, paranoia, being prone to mania or psychosis, who counts as trusted, coming back spaced out, stopping a medication or alcohol, and what you mix. Two paragraphs split where a second point starts: what to do when you can't tell what happened, after the paranoia examples and the THC line, and the medication warning, after coming back spaced out.
old: All kinds of psychoactive drugs can mess with your sense of what’s real, and that’s often the point of them, so you can break free of all your old patterns completely for a bit. But in general, try to select the healthiest ones and use slow and gentle protocols. I’d say one of the most abused psychedelics (aside from ketamine, if you call that a psychedelic) is 5-MeO-DMT. I have a guide on that. People very often believe you need a huge dose of it for a “full release.” They go through all kinds of screaming and shaking, nearly killing themselves, with absolutely zero inner-child work being done. It’s all spiritual bypassing.

Your own drug history matters too. If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don't try again until you understand what would make it safe. I’d look at the drug and the dosage, as well as mindset and setting etc.

Paranoia during a rough trip can be a warning sign for psychosis, but it doesn’t automatically lead there, since it can be valid. It tends to go that way when it isn’t balanced by practicality. “The CIA is mind-controlling me!” is paranoia. “The CIA, marketers, and other forces are conspiring to mind-control me, the way they do to everyone else! But since I can see that, I can prevent it to some extent, just by being aware of how it operates” is paranoia too, but it’s practically useful, and less likely to lead to psychosis. “...which means I can prevent it by standing on my head and counting backwards from 33, since 33 is their magic Freemason number!” is leaning psychotic. Some drugs are known for causing paranoia, like THC, so I’d avoid those. If you can’t clearly understand what happened yourself, get someone qualified to help. And if you have an idea of what happened but aren’t sure, ask someone who knows you well.

Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I'd be careful with other drugs that mess with what's real too. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it's family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. These are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can't, get help from trusted advisors.

By trusted, I mean someone you know is trustworthy from a long relationship with them, not someone people on Reddit said was super magical and healing. That's called a crapshoot. It might turn out well, it might not. It might seem like it did, and then later you realize you were duped, as happened to me with Sidney the iboga shaman. A new therapist is not as trusted as an old one. As they say, "new friends are silver, but old friends are gold."

Say you keep coming back from trips confused or spaced out. Maybe nothing worse happens, but after several trips like that I'd be concerned. If you're having episodes when you're sober, or any of them are severe, see a psychiatrist. And don't suddenly stop a medication just because you suspect it's involved. Talk to the doctor who prescribed it. Benzos can be dangerous to quit cold turkey. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous if you're physically dependent.

Be careful what you mix, too, and not just prescribed medicines. Even some basic things like cinnamon can be dangerous (and helpful) with ayahuasca, and doctors don't know about a lot of this. I also learned that mixing acacia confusa with mimosa hostilis is very destabilizing and challenging, but excellent if you want to know how it feels to be painfully autistic + schizo! I have a list of things to be cautious about with ayahuasca in particular.

sections.heading: # When the Adult Voice Feels Fake
sections.why: After Scott's line and your thoughts on why it can feel fake, each of the last three paragraphs is its own way through. Each heading is that paragraph's own first sentence or clause, so the paragraph starts right after it.
old: A lot of people get stuck right here. You call up the Nurturer and try to talk to your little one, and you get silence or a numb feeling, and all of a sudden your phone or the laundry feels urgent. Or some voice says this is silly, and it's hard to tell which part of you is saying it.
My friend Scott said:
> "Half the time when I try to connect to baby me, I feel fake and it seems crazy."

I used to be all personal trainer and teach persistence on this as the remedy. Keeping at it does help, since a little one who learned to expect being dropped won't trust you right away. But I don't think that explains the adult feeling fully. More importantly, I think it could even be like unintentional gaslighting to the little one to ask to connect with them when you don't believe they're even real. Like when my mom pretended to listen to me when I was young, but even less excusable (from the inner child's view) because she was not asking for my time when she did that. So, it's worth meditating first on why it feels fake.

Sometimes kindness feels scary more than fake. One study's title has a word for that: "compassion-threat." People in it with anxious or avoidant attachment reacted to compassion imagery like a threat, and a ten-minute exercise in feeling secure helped with the next try. Another found a first try at imagery like that "can be frightening for people who have a tendency to be self-critical." So feeling fake could mean you need a bridge, more than a bigger performance of love.

And picturing one ideal parent seems to help some people. There's a whole method built on it, called the Ideal Parent Figure method. In a small pilot, seventeen adults with complex PTSD from childhood trauma did five weeks of it and were still doing better eight months later. Seventeen people with nobody to compare them to won't prove the whole method, but it's a start.

For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state, like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn't prove they happened. I'd still hang on to what you felt, even once it's gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You've felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn't just pretending.

sections.heading: # Finding a Therapist to Borrow Adulthood
sections.why: After the first step, each paragraph is its own kind of help or its own question, so a reader looking for one of them can find it.
old: We all need some support, especially when taking our first steps. First and easiest is to start with finding a somatic therapist, if that resonates, as per my Somatic Therapies Guide.

Inner Child Reparenting therapists do exist, and you can find them, although they often are not licensed, and I don't know of any central directory, nor of any protocol they'd have in common. There are none which work with my guide yet. I can consult, and if you like the guide, you can ask a therapist to check it out and see what they agree with or disagree with as a great way to vet them.

The best licensed, listed therapists you'll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I'll talk more about those in the appendix, but Schema Therapy comes closest to my approach. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I'd especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won't tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I'd also want one who doesn't put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won't charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can't tell you any of that.

Regarding AI therapy, I've tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they're all pretty bad. I'm trying to make my own based on this guide, but I'm becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn't mean you can't get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, though, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes.

Does it keep ending the same way, where you bring up something that hurt and then still end up reassuring them they're not a bad person, and the talk never comes back to what happened to you? (The psychologist Lindsay Gibson wrote the book on this: *Disentangling from Emotionally Immature People*.) Or can they hear you disagree and look at their own part?

If it's the first, it can seem like you haven't explained yourself well enough yet. You probably have, and it makes more sense to count on what they keep showing you they can do than on the right words finally getting through to them. Maybe what they can do is text you something kind the next day and not bring any of it up.

You may not know for certain whether the other person is or could be capable of a healthier response, and neither do they. If they promise to change, that's probably as useful as their prior promises were. Think about how long it has taken you to become more healthy. Could you have done that from one moment to the next based on a promise? Sometimes we can be a better support for someone when we maintain a realistic boundary, so that we can hold high expectations, and still feel prepared for their failure to meet them.

sections.heading: ## Borrow One Competency at a Time
sections.why: After the idea (borrow one function at a time), each paragraph is one of the three jobs, so a reader who needs one of them can go straight there.
old: A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it's not just a foolish waste of time. It's actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there's always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
For warmth, think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it's someone who liked you the way you were.

For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you're about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you're about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that's ok. "Fake it til you make it" isn't exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, "I did that for us. That was the Protector." If it sounds funny, laugh!

The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That's a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like "What would Jesus do?" or "What would Buddha do?") can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

sections.heading: ### How Would You Know It's Helping?
sections.why: Its first paragraph is 210 words, the longest in the guide but one: the question to ask, the signs of progress, the parenting picture, and what therapy should do for your days. Each gets its own paragraph, every sentence kept.
old: Don't be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that's the endgame, it's just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It's like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don't need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn't as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.
If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live, stop there.

sections.heading: # How to Forgive Without Forgetting
sections.why: Its order stays: the first paragraph says before the practice that you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better, and the last answers it after. Only the last paragraph, 156 words, splits in two: that they still answer for it, and what can still be right.
old: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can't be put on a schedule. And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person's conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay. It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they'd never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody's limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."

And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

The understanding that helps me is seeing how a person's conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move they made. Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn't handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you've held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

They still have to answer for what they did, and it still hurt. Seeing how they got there doesn't make it okay. It's just that punishing them now can't reach back and give them what they were missing then, the sense to see it or the help. Or the skills. What's left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they'd never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody's limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."

sections.heading: ## Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care
sections.why: Your 109 A: Solomon's paradox is the name of the gap the trick gets around, that people reason more wisely about other people's problems than about their own, so the name goes on that; the rest of your sentence stays.
old: Sometimes it's not that you can't love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you've found the other one. But maybe you direct that love to your little one and the attempt goes flat, or starts to feel weirdly unsafe. Just feel that love you can feel for others for a minute, in your body, before you try to redirect anything. Then as you relax into that and enjoy it more, imagine it flowing downhill, like an overflowing river of delicious chocolate. Now imagine how happy your inner child is at the bottom of the hill to play in that chocolate love that rolled down!

Watch how it lands, though. "I care about you" can be patient, or it can be "I care about you, now hurry up and feel better." Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who's just sitting there. And if nothing moves at all, don't push it. Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you're borrowing something you already know how to do.

Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, all the conditions you face, and then step outside it and ask what you’d tell them as a friend. This psychological trick has a rich history around it, and even has a name, Solomon’s paradox, after the biblical king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.

Then take a small piece of whatever you'd tell them and hand it to yourself. If the advice was "get more sleep," then for now just try brushing your teeth before midnight instead of at two. That's how you learn as a kid, and it works now, too. The technical term for this is "scaffolding."
